comparisons.peer_topic: Payment Default Rates for Recent Consumer Real Estate TDRs
comparisons.peer_summary: The bank discloses the carrying value of consumer real estate loans that entered payment default during 2022 which had been modified in a TDR within the 12 months preceding the default; default is recognized after missing three monthly payments since modification, excluding loans with unpaid trial modification offers.
comparisons.comparison: Both Citigroup (C) and Bank of America (BAC) define specific performance criteria for re-aging or removing loans from troubled status after modification, though they focus on different loan types and metrics. C specifies a frequency limit for re-aging (once in 12 months, twice in five years) and relies on FFIEC guidelines for open-ended loans requiring three consecutive payments. In contrast, BAC focuses on consumer real estate TDRs, defining 'payment default' as missing three monthly payments (consecutively or not) after modification, which serves as a metric to track the stability of modified loans rather than the initial re-aging trigger. Both disclose structural constraints on loan modifications, but C emphasizes regulatory frequency caps and payment requirements for credit cards, while BAC emphasizes default tracking for real estate TDRs.

sentences.text: In addition, re-aging is subject to limitations, generally once in 12 months and twice in five years.

Specifically, re-aging practices for certain open-ended consumer loans, such as credit cards, are governed by Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council (FFIEC) guidelines, which require at least three consecutive minimum monthly payments or the equivalent amount, to be re-aged to current status.
A payment default for consumer real estate TDRs is recognized when a borrower has missed three monthly payments (not necessarily consecutively) since modification.

comparisons.peer_topic: Accounting treatment of distressed loan modifications
comparisons.peer_summary: Modified distressed loans are generally placed on nonaccrual status but may return to performing status if the borrower performs under modified terms for at least six months and repayment is reasonably assured.
comparisons.comparison: Citigroup (C) and JPMorgan Chase (JPM) both disclose the conditions under which modified consumer loans return to accrual or performing status, highlighting differences in performance periods. C states that loans are re-aged to current status upon permanent modification, subject to specific regulatory limits (FFIEC) and frequency caps. JPM explicitly details that loans modified as FDMs (financial difficulty modifications) are generally placed on nonaccrual status and require a minimum of six months of performance under modified terms to return to performing status. Both address the operational mechanics of 'returning' a loan to a current/performing state, but C implies immediate re-aging upon permanent modification (subject to constraints), whereas JPM enforces a specific six-month performance test before resuming interest accrual.

sentences.text: Upon permanent modification, the loan is re-aged to current status.
In addition, re-aging is subject to limitations, generally once in 12 months and twice in five years.
Loans, except for credit card loans, reported as FDMs are generally placed on nonaccrual status, although in many cases such loans were already on nonaccrual status prior to modification.

These loans may be returned to performing status (the accrual of interest is resumed) if the following criteria are met: (i) the borrower has performed under the modified terms for a minimum of six months and/or six payments, and (ii) the Firm has an expectation that repayment of the modified loan is reasonably assured based on, for example, the borrower's debt capacity and level of future earnings, collateral values, LTV ratios, and other current market considerations.
